title: Bookstore Checkout & Search
description: Design order state machines, payment integration, Elasticsearch for full-text book search, and collaborative filtering recommendation engines.

segments.text: The order state machine: created → payment_pending → payment_confirmed → fulfillment_processing → shipped → delivered. Each state has allowed transitions and side effects — payment_confirmed triggers inventory decrement, shipped triggers email notification. Failed payment moves to payment_failed with retry logic. Cancelled requires refund processing.

Payment integration uses a payment gateway like Stripe. Create a PaymentIntent with the order amount, collect card details via Stripe Elements on the frontend — card numbers never touch your server, minimizing PCI scope. Handle webhooks for async payment confirmation. Always verify the webhook signature to prevent spoofing.

Checkout must be atomic: validate cart items are in stock, calculate total with tax and shipping, process payment, create order record, decrement inventory. If any step fails, roll back previous steps. Use the Saga pattern — each step has a compensating action. Payment fails? Release inventory reservation. Inventory unavailable? Don't charge the card.

Elasticsearch powers full-text book search. Index fields: title, author, description, ISBN, categories, publisher. Use multi_match queries for relevance across fields — boost title matches three times over description matches. Add fuzzy matching for typos, synonym expansion for related terms, and faceted navigation for filtering by category, price range, and rating.

A user searches 'harry potter' but your catalog has it listed as 'Harry Potter and the Philosopher\'s Stone'. How does your search handle partial title matches, different editions, and series grouping?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you handle partial title matches, multiple editions, and series grouping in book search?

segments.text: Search autocomplete uses an edge-ngram analyzer. Index 'Harry Potter' as 'h', 'ha', 'har', 'harr', 'harry'. When the user types 'har', match against the edge-ngrams for instant suggestions. Limit to ten suggestions, sorted by popularity. Cache the top one thousand queries in Redis for sub-millisecond autocomplete response.

Collaborative filtering: users who bought book A also bought book B. Build a co-purchase matrix from order history. For a given book, find books with the highest co-purchase frequency. Amazon's 'customers also bought' drives thirty-five percent of their revenue. Start simple — item-item collaborative filtering — before investing in complex ML models.

Order tracking provides visibility into fulfillment. Events: order_placed, payment_processed, picked, packed, label_created, shipped, out_for_delivery, delivered. Each event has a timestamp and optional location. Push updates via email and in-app notifications. Partner with carriers for tracking data via API — FedEx, UPS, and USPS all provide tracking webhooks.

Book reviews need moderation. Allow verified purchasers to leave reviews — link review to order. Prevent review bombing with rate limits — one review per book per user. Sort by helpfulness votes, not recency. Flag reviews with profanity or off-topic content for manual review. Amazon's Vine program provides trusted early reviews for new releases.

Design the complete checkout and search system for an online bookstore with five million titles, one hundred thousand orders per day, and sub-two-hundred-millisecond search latency. What are your key architectural decisions?
segments.thought_prompt: Design checkout + search for 5M titles, 100K orders/day, sub-200ms search. Architecture?

segments.text: Bookstore checkout uses order state machines with Saga-based compensation, payment gateway integration for PCI compliance, and Elasticsearch for rich full-text search with autocomplete. Recommendations via collaborative filtering drive significant revenue. The system combines transactional correctness for orders with search relevance for discovery.
